title: ESDC Wellness Gym: SharePoint Redesign
job: UX Design & Research, ESDC (AI & Service Design, FSWEP)

star.situation: The Workplace Mental Health team's intranet site couldn't be updated without IT, and it was hard to organize the growing catalogue of resources the team wanted to make available.
star.task: Move the website from the ESDC legacy intranet to SharePoint so the team maintains it directly and 40,000 employees can find resources more easily.
star.action: I ran early-stage exploratory moderated interviews to understand how employees reach for mental-health resources and built personas. I also tested the proposed Information Architecture with two rounds of treejack testing (29 participants). I facilitated two group design workshops with the team to ensure I incorporated the early-stage research into a prototype. While away from the project, a colleague completed the remaining work and facilitated later-stage usability testing on the new pages. I rejoined the initiative in the last month pre-deployment to work on the last few iterations of the webpages.
star.result: The revised architecture shipped as a working SharePoint site the team owns and updates without IT tickets, with an FAQ for employees new to SharePoint.

title: ESDC AI Implementation & Enablement
job: UX Design & Research, ESDC (AI & Service Design, FSWEP)

star.situation: A federal workplace wellness team had access to AI tools but no clear way to adopt them.
star.task: Test the tools and help the team use them well.
star.action: I tested agentic AI and RAG systems, designed personalized AI workflows for the team, and aligned the approach with the psychological factors behind healthy workplace adoption. I wrote training resources, reference guides, and process documentation so colleagues could use the tools without me in the room.

title: City of Calgary: Digital Equity Pilot

star.situation: Calgary funded a pilot to test seven essential digital services with the residents most affected by the digital divide: newcomers, older adults, and people with disabilities who use assistive tech. People who use assistive technology were the hardest to reach because our screening had specific criteria: testers had to be able to test independently and could not be professional testers. While overseeing three other projects, this one landed on my plate behind schedule with about four weeks to finish.
star.task: Recruit, organize and run usability testing across five participant groups, thirty-seven people in total, and coordinate a team of twenty to a tight deadline.
star.action: I built a referral program with monetary incentives and sent personalized outreach for snowball recruitment. For assistive tech users, small operational details mattered. I offered to walk people through our intake form by phone. I also found that our Google Form did not play well with text-to-speech on iPhone and Mac, so I documented the issue and worked around it. Pre-interviews surfaced that several screen reader users preferred their phones, so I pushed to relax the desktop-only rule with the City testing team.
star.result: We mapped eighteen equity challenges across all seven services, the City proposed a follow-up round that added mobile testing, and one participant became an advocate who went on to refer others. The findings are still discussed across the City's digital teams.

star.situation: Calgary Economic Development's work-integrated learning program built a website and employer portal to connect students with placements, with part of the portal run by a third-party vendor.
star.task: Evaluate usability and inclusiveness and hand back fixes the client would actually act on.
star.action: As program manager and UXR I coordinated and assisted in moderated remote sessions with scripts adapted per user group. We also did a heuristic pass and accessibility testing with a screen reader user, thirteen participants across the two phases. When one phase came up short of the tester criteria I wanted, I was upfront with the client and tried to recruit more, though those additions cancelled. Reading that the client had no time for a dense document, I led with an executive summary and a presentation, and we prioritized fixes with an impact-effort matrix tied to their constraints. After vendor limitations surfaced late on more than one project, meaning our recommendations were not within the client's control, I rebuilt our client intake to ask about third-party tools up front.
star.result: We delivered usability and heuristic findings across both phases on time, in a format the client could move on quickly, and the intake change meant later projects scoped vendor limits correctly from the start.

star.situation: IncluCity ran inclusive research for municipal, nonprofit, and social-impact clients, with researchers of varying experience and no shared operating system at the start.
star.task: Build the operations layer that lets a volunteer-heavy research org deliver consistent, high-quality work at scale, and grow the organization's capabilities in its inclusive research services.
star.action: I built a research-operations framework for 50+ researchers covering onboarding, training, data management, and QA. I supported proposals and client acquisition from first contact through delivery, and ran inclusive-design workshops and panels.
star.result: The framework standardized how projects ran across the org. I organized 140+ interviews, contributed to a number of client-ready reports, and our inclusive-design events reached 100+ attendees.

title: Beneva: Online Quote Evaluation
job: UX Researcher, HEC UX Evaluation (pro bono)

star.situation: Beneva, one of Canada's largest mutual insurers, wanted to know where its online quote flow lost users.
star.task: As part of a four-person team, evaluate the home and auto quote experiences and rank what to fix first.
star.action: We ran moderated usability tests with surveys, scored the experience using validated scales and rated each finding by severity. The clearest failure showed up when participants edited a home quote. Six of twelve were unable to finish the quoting process. My main contributions were the study design and the quantitative analysis.
star.result: We delivered a report that combined primary user research with secondary market research to benchmark against competitors. We recommended eight major fixes and several minor ones, each with severity ratings and an impact-by-effort matrix.

title: Tech3Lab: GenAI Tutoring Study (Thesis + FLAIRS)
methods: Multimodal physiological measurement (eye-tracking, pupillometry, EEG, ECG)

star.situation: I had spent months preparing a neuroadaptive study built on a biocybernetic feedback loop. A week before data collection, the specially designed EEG set the whole design depended on broke. The lab time, the participant pool, and the testing window were already committed.
star.task: Rebuild a study that could still answer a real question about AI-mediated learning, use the equipment we had left, and hold up as both a thesis and a publication. The window would not move.
star.action: I went back to the literature and found the open question I could still answer with available instrumentation: AI tutors personalize learning, but there was little direct evidence of how that personalization changes a learner's cognitive load in real time. With the team's support, I redesigned the study inside a week, from research question through ethics, then ran it, capturing eye-tracking, pupillometry, ECG, and EEG while participants worked through AI-mediated math tasks. I analyzed behavioural and physiological data together to read cognitive load rather than relying on self-report.
star.result: The study became my master's thesis and a FLAIRS conference publication, with design recommendations for AI tutor systems. The finding held: quiz scores stayed flat while pupil dilation dropped, meaning learners with a personalized AI processed the same material under less cognitive load.

title: UQAM SEXODEV: Workflow Automation
methods: AI workflow design (recordings → tasks / summaries / docs)

star.situation: A research chair and her small remote team were buried in manual overload.
star.task: Diagnose the bottlenecks and build a system that cuts that load and improves accountability.
star.action: I started with stakeholder interviews to find where work actually stalled, then designed AI-driven workflows that turn meeting recordings into assigned tasks, individual action summaries, and filed documentation. I set up automations to help with note-taking during meetings, personalized participant survey distribution and research communication. I also presented on organizational changes that could help the team.
star.result: The team replaced manual note-taking with an automated pipeline and consolidated scattered files into one organized workspace.

title: Allen & Thomas: E-Discovery AI
job: AI Search & Implementation Specialist (Contractor), Allen & Thomas LLP

star.situation: A law firm needed to search and review a large document database (E-discovery) across a remote team, and needed a way to coordinate the search and quickly learn to use the database search tools available.
star.task: Set up a system to improve how the database was searched and initiate tools to help with this process.
star.action: I implemented a systematic search process considering many constraints/requirements and implemented various forms of AI as search tools (applied supervised learning to rank documents for review). I coordinated the search across the team by setting up a Notion workspace with onboarding guides so the process survives staff turnover.
star.result: The team was able to share findings more quickly, search more efficiently while working remotely and understand how to use the database platform with the information in my Notion page.

title: Notion to AI to Anki Pipeline

star.situation: My course notes lived in Notion as text, tables, and lecture screenshots. I love flashcards for studying, but the digital ones cost money and I did not always have time to make them, and I did not want to give up spaced repetition on the go.
star.task: Point an open-source study card tool (Anki) at a Notion page and get reviewed spaced-repetition cards out the other end, while staying in control of what I study.
star.action: I wrote the architecture as a spec first, then directed Claude Code to build a two-stage pipeline. Stage one reads the full page and screenshots and sends them to a vision model that returns atomic Q&A cards, which land in a review file I prune. Stage two loads the approved cards into Anki through AnkiConnect.
star.result: The first run produced 58 accurate cards from 1,876 content blocks and 137 screenshots for about two cents, and the model derived 25 hierarchical week tags on its own from my lecture headings. None needed deleting. The manual step that kept me off spaced repetition is gone, and the review checkpoint stayed in by design.

star.task: Provide consistent programming and accessible events as Co-director of the organization. In summary, running events and building the community.

star.result: Our first two events drew strong interest, with over 200 people signalling they wanted to attend. Speakers joined from Qatar, Ottawa, and Montreal, spanning academia, ex-Meta, and private consulting.

star.situation: Complete Complaints Foundation was validating a new website across five user segments and wanted to know how each group read the initial design before beta. We had no tester pool of our own and depended on the client's contact list, which meant rebooking sessions several times as the client's timeline slipped.
star.task: Organize testing schedule for moderated usability testing that surfaced barriers per segment (language, accessibility, navigation) and hand back prioritized, usable findings on a compressed schedule.
star.action: I ran project operations and organized eight virtual sessions, where I edited a dynamic script that swapped in segment-specific questions for each user segment group. I paired the sessions with an accessibility pass and a quantitative survey.
star.result: Testing showed the site carried too much text and scrolling, that the search bar needed to be more prominent, and that terms like "Insights" and the partner-versus-sponsor distinction confused people. The client left with concrete design fixes: cut copy, surface search, and differentiate buttons from tags.

title: BRDGE: Usability Evaluation

star.situation: BRDGE, a food-ordering startup, wanted usability testing that would also teach their team to run research themselves. The engagement drifted from the statement of work I had proposed. The client kept changing the script and the site mid-project and stayed heavily involved in moderating sessions, which added load onto a small, low-budget team already short on leads.
star.task: Deliver credible findings on the ordering experience while managing a client who wanted hands-on control of the research.
star.action: I stepped into the lead role and brought on more volunteers, delegating the work so a small team could still ship. We ran seven moderated sessions with a heuristic and accessibility pass, then reported findings as a simplified user journey the client could act on without wading through a long deck.
star.result: The findings held up. Participants who hit bad design also reported lower trust in the service, and confusion over portion sizes, prices, and product photos left people unsure about their orders, which pointed at the information hierarchy as the core problem. The lesson I carried forward is that client-moderated sessions bias results regardless of the client's UX training, and it changed how I scoped client involvement in later projects.

title: University of Calgary Active Living: Usability Evaluation

star.situation: The University of Calgary's Active Living site and registration portal carried three heavy processes: equipment rentals, program signups, and class registration. The client wanted to know how a diverse set of users moved through them and where navigation, language, or accessibility got in the way.
star.task: Test all three flows across diverse user groups and staff a large project through volunteer turnover.
star.action: I split coverage across two scripts that each started at a different entry point and reached more of the site together than one session could, then ran twelve remote facilitated sessions with six testers per group, including a screen reader user. On the operations side, the project's size strained team lead retention, so I managed staffing and handoffs to keep sessions moving.
star.result: Testers struggled to find membership information, their cart, and course availability, and hit confusion in the booking and rental steps. The screen reader user met unlabeled links and sections that were hard to move through. The finding that traveled furthest was that pricing and program details only appeared after account login, which gave people a reason to abandon signup before they had enough to decide.

star.situation: Platform Calgary ran usability testing across two phases, and by phase two we were bringing back participants from phase one to see how the experience had changed. The client wanted to pack more into each session than an hour allowed.
star.task: Hold the line on session quality while keeping a delayed project from eating into the resources other IncluCity projects needed.
star.action: I pushed back on lengthening the sessions and explained the reasoning: past about an hour, participant attention drops and answer quality falls with it, so stretching the script only trades data quality for a couple more tasks. We kept sessions tight, ran twelve participants in phase one and eight in phase two with two returning, and I managed the schedule so the client's delays did not pull staff off other work.
star.result: The client got cleaner data from focused sessions and a phase-over-phase read on the same participants, and IncluCity's other projects kept their people and timelines.

star.situation: On a YWCA evaluation, I staffed a team lead I rated highly. The deliverable had shifted from what we scoped; outside pressures were mounting, and she reached a point where she no longer felt she could commit to the role, which was completely understandable.
star.task: Keep the project moving and find another team lead for the project.
star.action: I moved her off the lead role, brought in more team members to cover the gap, and went back to the client to ask for more time rather than ship late or thin. Afterward I sat down with her to hear how it had gone from her side, and I owned that I had not brought her perspective into the plan as early as I should have.
star.result: We delivered a PURE and heuristic evaluation on the revised timeline. The bigger return was operational. I started bringing leads into timeline and scope conversations from the start and set expectations with clients earlier. I also got more honest with myself about how to estimate timelines. Asking for more time is fine when you flag it early.

star.situation: Chic Geek, a Calgary nonprofit in the women-in-tech space, was one of my earliest projects at IncluCity. It was where I learned how the organization ran day to day, from its volunteer community to how projects moved from scoping to a client readout.
star.task: Contribute to a usability evaluation while getting up to speed on IncluCity's people and process.
star.action: I worked project operations alongside two other overlapping projects, on an eight-participant moderated usability study, from recruitment and scheduling through to the final presentation, and used it to understand how a volunteer-heavy research team coordinates real client work.
star.result: The study delivered on schedule, and the grounding I got here in how IncluCity operated set up the operations work I took on across later projects.

star.situation: Shift was recruiting for a long-term study, the kind that asks participants to stay engaged and check in every few months. The population was specific and vulnerable, so a poor match would drop out partway and cost the study time it could not spare.
star.task: Recruit, screen, and onboard participants who would stay the course, working as a team of one.
star.action: I owned recruitment from end to end. I pre-screened against tight criteria, then walked each candidate through what a multi-month commitment with recurring check-ins actually asked of them, so people signed on knowing what they were agreeing to. Retention over that timeline came down to fit, so I focused on the screening process.
star.result: I delivered eleven screened, prepared participants matched to the study's population and set up to stay engaged through its check-in cycle.

star.situation: Rainforest was the largest qualitative study IncluCity had run to that point, around twenty participants, which was more than double our usual recruitment effort. That scale made both the logistics and the volume of data harder to manage cleanly. Each participant group focused on a different object plus one shared object, which let us compare across groups.
star.task: Recruit and run a study at a size the team had not handled before, and keep the data organized enough to report on.
star.action: I led recruitment for the twenty participants and set up Coda for the first time to manage participants and testing data as the study grew. Getting the data structure right up front was what kept a study this size from turning into a pile we could not sort later.
star.result: We ran and reported the study, and the recruitment and data-management setup I built here carried into how I ran recruitment and data on later projects. This work is also how I first connected with Rainforest, which later brought me on directly as a project management contractor (see the Rainforest Alberta coordinator card).
